full_judgment:
21. The learned Additional Attorney General has harped on the theme that once it is vested property which had been exempted from attachment, seizure or sale in execution of the Civil Court decree the executability of such decree ceases is benefit of substance because that negates the effect of Ordinance No. 93 of 1976 There is no magic in the word "vested". It has not got any fixed connotation. It depends upon user of such expression in a particular piece of legislation. It may vest in title or it may vest in any position or it may vest in a limited sense. That the word 'vested' means a different thing in different context can be seen from cursory glance in numerable statutes. When the property is vested in the receiver under the Insolvency Act it vests only for a limited purpose and the receiver cannot have any interest of his own in the property vide section 56 of the Insolvency Act, 1920. On the other hand, there are some statutes which say that the property so required upon the happening of certain events shall "vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances." See sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act 1894, Here the legislature had made it clear that the vesting of property is not for any limited period or limited duration. In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act all land vested in the Government after the abolition of rent receiving interest vested absolutely and not for a limited period. When the land vested under paragraph 8 of the Administration and Disposal Order 1966 it was only for a limited purpose. Ordinance 93 of 1976 being the latest legislative will displaces the bar given by temporary law and as such that will no longer be available for resisting the decree to be put into execution. In this view of the matter, to my mind there is no force in the contention of the learned Additional Attorney General. Hence I agree with my brother S Ahmed, J that this appeal should be allowed and the order of the High Court Division should be set-aside whereupon the execution case should be disposed of in accordance with law. 

 Rule 182 was among those Rules which were thus continued in force even after the abrogation of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance. The Administration and Disposal Order (1966) therefore continued in force automatically as Rule 182 continued in force, there having been no necessity for a separate legislation for this purpose. After emergence of Bangladesh as an independent State, Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 was repealed by Act XLV of 1974 namely, the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency) (Repeal) Act. This Repealing Act in section 3(1) provides, inter alia, that "all enemy property vested in the Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the Defence of Pakistan Rules as continued in force—"shall vest in the government". This section was amended by Ordinance No.93 of 1976 which provides that the enemy property vested in the government shall be administered, controlled, managed or disposed of by transfer or otherwise by the Government. Section 3(1) of the Repealing Act, with this amendment, reads thus: 

 28. The learned Additional Attorney General has lastly contended that when the property has already been vested in the Government, it cannot be divested by sale or otherwise and consequently the decree for sale of the land cannot be executed. The learned Additional Attorney General has however failed to cite any law which prohibits disposal by transfer of any property vested in the Government. The property being vested in the Government, their authority to deal with it has been rather strengthened. It may be mentioned here that with the abolition of all rent-receiving interests in land under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, all land vested in the Government who thereby got absolute power to dispose of land in any manner, such as sale, lease settlement. The contention of the learned Additional Attorney General that a vested property cannot be disposed of by sale has got no substance. We therefore upheld the contention of Mr Paul that with the repeal of Defence of Pakistan Rules, the Administration and Disposal Order made thereunder also stood repealed. The bar to the execution of the decree passed in favour of the appellant, I find, has been removed. The decree is found to be quite executable. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the impugned order of the High Court Division along with the order of the Executing Court is set aside and it is directed that the Execution Case No. 4 of 1967 be disposed of in the light of this judgment. No order as to cost.
